splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's or an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous guideline/statute that expands criminal liability, or whether the rule of lenity should prevail and resolve the ambiguity in the defendant's favor. This split has significant implications for criminal sentencing and the balance between agency interpretive power and protections for criminal defendants.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, requiring ambiguities to be resolved in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous guidelines to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether USSG § 4B1.2(b)'s definition of 'controlled substance offense' includes inchoate offenses such as conspiracy and attempt, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses like conspiracy to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation deserving deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This split affects career-offender designations and significantly impacts sentencing ranges for drug offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to deference as an authoritative interpretation of the guideline, and thus inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to the definition rather than interpreting it, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for drug offenders depending on geography, as it determines eligibility for sentences below statutory minimums.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that the word 'and' means defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, so meeting only one or two does not bar relief.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as effectively meaning 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under USSG § 4B1.2(b) when the state schedule covers substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's reference to 'an offense under . . . state law' requires the underlying substance to also be federally scheduled, or whether any state-scheduled substance qualifies. This split affects career-offender designations and base offense levels for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances like certain marijuana analogs that may not be federally controlled.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes any offense under state law, without requiring the specific substance to be controlled under federal law.

positions.label: Federal schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law, requiring a categorical match to the federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under the compassionate release statute. Some circuits hold that such changes are categorically excluded, while others permit courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to authorize this, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be extraordinary and compelling
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the totality of circumstances in determining whether extraordinary and compelling reasons exist for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs after a Chapter 13 filing but before conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate based on the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), while other circuits have reached the opposite conclusion. This split has major implications for debtors considering conversion and for the value available to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a), post-petition pre-conversion increases in property value belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the structure, purpose, and legislative history of § 348(f), post-petition pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, when conversion is in good faith.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) rather than civil rights statutes (e.g., Bivens) to challenge Bureau of Prisons decisions regarding conditions of confinement, including First Step Act earned time credit determinations.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the terms or conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement). Some circuits require habeas for any claim that could affect release timing, while others permit civil rights or other statutory actions. This split affects thousands of federal prisoners seeking to challenge BOP administrative decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges a BOP decision that affects the duration of confinement or timing of release, habeas corpus under § 2241 is the sole federal remedy, precluding civil rights or other statutory actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may pursue civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or § 1983) to challenge conditions of confinement even when the challenged decision may incidentally affect release timing, and habeas is not the exclusive remedy for such claims.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release for the purpose of punishing the defendant for the violation of supervised release conditions, or only to sanction the original offense.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the purpose of a revocation sentence is to punish the defendant for the breach of trust or violation of supervised release conditions, or whether it must be limited to sanctioning the original underlying offense. The Sixth Circuit permits punishment for the violation itself, while other circuits limit the focus to the original offense. This affects how courts determine appropriate sentences at revocation hearings.

positions.label: May punish for the violation itself
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions, treating the breach of trust as a separately punishable event.

positions.label: Must focus on the original offense, not the violation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must be grounded in the seriousness of the original offense and the defendant's characteristics, not as punishment for the supervised release violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the deadline to appeal a Hyde Amendment order for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days under FRAP 4(a)) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days under FRAP 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter for purposes of the appellate deadline. The majority of circuits apply the civil deadline, treating the fee motion as ancillary to the criminal case, but there is a split on the correct characterization. This affects whether appeals from Hyde Amendment denials are timely.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under FRAP 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises within a criminal case, the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under FRAP 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA and MPPAA require that actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability be fixed as of the end of the plan year preceding the withdrawal, or whether the actuary may select or update assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined and fixed by the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), providing greater predictability for employers.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond what was specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for individuals who flee supervision.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, so the supervision period does not run while the supervisee is a fugitive.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that federal courts lack authority to toll supervised release terms without explicit statutory authorization, so the supervision period continues to run even during absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether the gatekeeping provision of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, or whether such prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law. This affects access to collateral review for thousands of federal prisoners.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements without the additional categorical bar.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election rules such as mail-in ballot counting deadlines. The split concerns whether competitive injury from allegedly unlawful ballots is sufficiently concrete and imminent to confer standing before the election occurs, or whether such claims are too speculative.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when state election rules allegedly dilute lawful votes or change the rules under which the election is conducted.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged competitive injury from post-Election-Day ballot counting is too speculative to confer Article III standing for pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine of 28 U.S.C. § 1291.
splits.description: Circuits have not uniformly addressed whether the denial of a motion to seal medical records in litigation constitutes a collateral order subject to immediate appellate review. The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, recognizing that delayed review risks irreparable harm once private information is disclosed. This approach may conflict with circuits applying a narrower view of the collateral order doctrine for sealing motions.

positions.label: Immediately appealable as collateral order
positions.summary: Holds that the denial of a motion to seal medical records is effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment and involves a value of high order (medical privacy), satisfying the collateral order doctrine for immediate appeal.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means such as protective orders or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to legal questions governing how business operators must treat customers and what remedies are available for discrimination or unfair treatment was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review, suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied standards for discrimination liability and damages in hospitality contexts that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or divergent from other circuits to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims and available remedies in the hospitality or business establishment context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
